text: Birendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev (Nepali: श्री ५ महाराजाधिराज वीरेन्द्र वीर विक्रम शाह देव; 29 December 1945 – 1 June 2001) was King of Nepal from 1972 until his assassination in 2001. He was the second son of King Mahendra and became crown prince because Mahendra's first son, Rabindra Shah, was born out of wedlock to a Gurung woman, making him an "illegitimate child." Birendra was born at the Narayanhiti Royal Palace in Kathmandu and became crown prince upon his grandfather King Tribhuvan's death in 1955. He studied at St Joseph's School in Darjeeling and later at Eton College in the United Kingdom from 1959 to 1964, before returning to Nepal to travel to remote villages. He then studied at the University of Tokyo and political theory at Harvard University from 1967 to 1968. Birendra married Aishwarya Rajya Lakshmi Devi, his second cousin, on 27 February 1970; the wedding cost $9.5 million and was one of the most lavish Hindu nuptial ceremonies in history. He ascended the throne on 31 January 1972 at age 26, with his coronation delayed until 24 February 1975, when he was 29, due to mourning and religious inauspiciousness traditions. As an absolute monarch, he inherited the panchayat system, which banned political parties; prominent leaders of the Nepali Congress were frequently arrested. In the 1980s, liberal student-led groups demanded constitutional change, and in May 1980, a referendum was held offering a multi-party or panchayati system, with the party-less system winning 55% to 45%. Following this, Birendra restructured the country into five development regions and visited each annually until 1990. In April 1990, after pro-democracy riots, he lifted the ban on political parties and agreed to become a constitutional monarch, appointing a Constitution Recommendation Commission that presented a draft constitution on 10 September 1990. The draft was approved by Prime Minister Krishna Prasad Bhattarai and his cabinet, and on 9 November 1990, Birendra promulgated the new constitution, transforming Nepal into a constitutional monarchy with multiparty democracy. As a constitutional monarch, he gained popularity due to his democratic views and the inability of political parties to govern. However, he could not prevent the Nepalese Civil War, which lasted from 1996 to 2006. On 1 June 2001, Birendra and his family were massacred by his son, Crown Prince Dipendra, during a dinner at the Narayanhiti Palace; after shooting himself, Dipendra was declared king but failed to regain consciousness and died days later. Birendra's younger brother Gyanendra then became king. During his reign, Birendra maintained Nepal's independence despite influences from India, China, and the Soviet Union. His first trips as king were to India in October 1973 and China two months later. He prevented the breakup of Mustang from Nepal and Tibet, disarmed Khampas rebels in the north by offering land, money, and citizenship to those who surrendered arms and confiscating weapons, and prohibited movement toward Tibet for those who did not surrender. He blocked the use of the army to suppress the Maoist revolution, which would have worsened the situation. Birendra was a lover of nature and a strong supporter of conservation. He established the Rhino Patrol force in 1970, introduced National Park law, and gazetted Chitwan National Park in December 1970 with borders delineated the following year and established in 1973. In 1976, he established Royal Karnali Wildlife Reserve (later Royal Bardiya), added Babai River Valley in 1984, and proclaimed it a national park in 1988. The fourth protected area, Langtang National Park, was established in 1976 with a 1,710 km² area in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, and Sindhulpalchok. He also established Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve and Royal Shuklaphanta Wildlife Reserve in 1976, which were later enlarged and converted to national parks in the late 1980s. Rara National Park was established in 1976 to fulfill his father's dream of a pristine reserve with a 106 km² area in Mugu and Jumla, including Rara Lake. Sagarmatha National Park was established in 1976 with a 1,148 km² area in Solukhumbu. In 1984, Khaptad National Park (225 km²) was established in Bajhang, Bajura, Achham, and Doti, and Parsa Wildlife Reserve was established and later extended to a national park. Shey Phoksundo National Park, a trans-Himalayan park of 3,555 km² in Dolpa and Mugu, was also established in 1984. To preserve royal hunting traditions and prevent wildlife depletion, he established Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve in 1987. The King Mahendra Trust for Nature Conservation was established in 1990 with Gyanendra as chairman, and he declared the Annapurna Conservation Area. Under his efforts, Sagarmatha National Park (1979) and Chitwan National Park (1984) were inscribed in UNESCO World Heritage Sites, along with the Durbar squares of Kathmandu, Lalitpur, and Bhaktapur, and religious sites such as Swayambhunath, Boudhanath, Pashupatinath, and Changu Narayan in 1979. On 28 December 1975, a trolley bus system was established with Chinese aid. He followed his father by establishing industrial estates: Nepalgunj (1973), Pokhara (1974), Butwal (1976), Bhaktapur (1979), Dhankuta (1980), Birendranagar (1981), and Gajendranarayan (1986). Birendra is credited with devising the Melamchi water project to Kathmandu. Industries such as Gorakhali Tires, Udayapur Cement, Nepal Metal, and Nepal Pharmaceuticals were established during his reign. He was the patron of the Pashupati Area Development Trust. In April 1979, the Nepal Oriental Magnesite factory was established with joint investment from Nepal and Orissa Industries, India, at Lakuri Danda in Dolakha. In 1983, a Nepal-Pakistan Joint Economic Commission was established, bringing significant foreign investment. A 60 megawatt hydropower project at Kulekhani began operation in 1982 with aid from the World Bank, Kuwait, and Japan. TU Teaching Hospital was established in 1982 with support from Japan International Cooperation Agency. Nardevi Ayurvedic Hospital was established in 1974, and the Nepal Police Hospital was established on 27 Chaitra 2040 BS to provide free health services to police and their families. In 1976, he established Securities Exchange Center Ltd, which later evolved into the Nepal Stock Exchange. He also established Nepal Television in 1984, which launched its first channel in 1985 with French aid. By 1986, there were 2,054 industrial establishments employing about 125,000 workers. By 1990, television reach made video rental and satellite dishes common. In 1986, with Rastriya Panchayat approval, Mahendra Sanskrit University was established in Dang, becoming the second university in the country. Studies in 1972 showed that road connectivity in hilly and rural areas was more expensive than air connectivity, leading the government to prioritize airport development. Airports such as Baglung (1973), Dhorpatan, Mahendranagar, Rukum Chaurjahari, Sanphebagar (1975), Simikot (1977), Dolpa (1978), Ramechhap (1979), Doti (1973), Talcha (1975), Taplejung (1976), Rolpa (1980), Manang (1981), Bajura (1984), and Darchula (1986) were established. The Lamosangu-Jiri road to Solukhumbu was commissioned in 1985 with Swiss aid. The government focused on agriculture, with nearly 90% of the population involved by 1990. Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper was established in 1985 with Chinese support. Corn production increased from 500,000 tons in 1961 to over 1 million tons in 1991. Lumbini Sugar Mills at Sunwal, Nawalparasi was built in 1982 with Chinese technical assistance. Gorakhali Rubber Industries led to rubber cultivation in Jhapa, Illam, and other eastern areas. Agricultural-based industries such as Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper, Hetauda Textile, and numerous carpet and garment industries were established, contributing significantly to the economy. A referendum in 2037 BS (equivalent to 1980 in the Gregorian calendar) was held for democracy, offering a multi-party or panchayati system. During the panchayati system option, the referendum was held in May 1980.

In 1985, under the Companies Act 2021 (Bikram Sambat) with support from the People's Republic of China, agricultural lands and the agricultural workforce expanded, leading to increased food supplies and improved nutrition. Corn production rose from 500,000 tons in 1961 to over 1 million tons by 1991. The Lumbini Sugar Mills at Sunwal, Nawalparasi was established in 1982 with technical assistance from China. The Gorakhali Rubber Industries led to the first cultivation of rubber in Jhapa, Illam, and other eastern regions of Nepal. Agriculture-based industries such as Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper, Hetauda Textile, and numerous carpet and garment industries were established to process raw agricultural products, significantly contributing to the economy. During King Birendra’s reign, a referendum was held in 2037 BS to choose between a multi-party system or a Panchayati system. To promote balanced development, he divided the nation into five development regions and visited each annually until the 1990 democracy movement, after which the visits ceased. Despite being an autocratic ruler, King Birendra adhered strictly to constitutional limits, acting as a constitutional monarch and intervening during political crises. Mid-term elections in 2051 and the general election in 2056 are attributed to his good governance. He regularly sought the Supreme Court’s advice on constitutional matters and established a weekly meeting between the king and prime minister at his palace to discuss state affairs. Recognizing low literacy as a major barrier to progress, he prioritized education, with the five-year plan from 1971 focusing on building new institutions and improving the education system. On the occasion of his coronation, he declared primary education free for all Nepalese citizens. In 1978, with royal approval, all educational materials were distributed free of cost. He became the patron of the Royal Nepal Academy of Science and Technology and established Mahendra Sanskrit University in 1986 to preserve language and culture. The dowry system was criminalized in 1976 under the Social Practices Reform Act (2033 B.S.). Under the five-year plan, he introduced National Service, requiring post-graduate students to serve one year in rural development. He initiated the preservation of history by establishing the Natural History Museum in 1975 and enacted the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 2033 (1976) to prohibit drug trade, smuggling, and trafficking. Birendra promoted road development based on population and traffic, connecting rural areas with airports, and restructured governmental organizations to achieve developmental goals, emphasizing roadbuilding, sanitation, and technical training. A comprehensive study led to the restructuring of the National Planning Commission in 1972 and minor adjustments in 1987. Government policies focused on environment conservation, agriculture, and education. Though remembered as a development-friendly ruler, he is criticized for lacking the skills to drive rapid development, similar to his father King Mahendra, and his emphasis on sustainable development—such as nature conservation, culture, and history—was seen as hindering economic progress. The Panchayat regime under Birendra is considered a failure by historians, as he failed to attract significant foreign investment and implemented reforms that continued his father’s legacy. He restructured organizations established by his father and introduced development plans envisioned by him. However, his development efforts largely failed, with many newly built roads and airports being rarely used due to low vehicle ownership or access, thus not contributing to economic growth. Some historians and anti-egalitarians blame Birendra for the fall of the Panchayat regime, as the easing of restrictions in the 1980s allowed previously powerless political parties to emerge. From a young age, Birendra was described by his Eton teachers as a kind prince and was remembered by classmates as a "very, very nice bloke" who was embarrassed when his full title was read aloud. Nepalese media personality Neer Shah described him as a kind and development-loving king. Royalists and scholars view him as a simple king who listened to others’ views, though they criticize his weakness in refusing requests from others and his tendency to work like a clerk rather than delegate. In 2036 B.S. (1980), he allowed the Janmat Sangraha referendum, seen as a step toward democracy, though leaders and historians claim it was rigged. After the People's Movement I, he established a constitutional monarchy in Nepal. Some historians speculate that his democratic views and simple nature contributed to the success of the People's Movement I (1990). He is credited with introducing SAARC to strengthen Nepal’s foreign relations with South Asian countries. Birendra was diagnosed with coronary artery disease; in November 1999, he suffered a mild heart attack and was admitted to Cromwell Hospital in London, where he underwent angioplasty. Numerous structures, institutions, and honors were named after him. Monuments bearing his name were renamed after the restoration of parliament in 2006 and the end of the monarchy in 2008. Following the 2006 political changes, an effort was made to rename the highway built in his honor as Lok Marg.
